code.title: Constructor injection with a tiny container

followUps:
Constructor injection makes a class impossible to build without its dependencies, so it can never be half-ready. The fields can be final, which also makes the object safe to share between threads.

It also helps tests: new OrderService(fakeNotifier) needs no Spring, no reflection and no container start. And a constructor with eight parameters is a visible warning that the class does too much.

Spring fails at startup with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException when two beans match and nothing says which to use. You then pick one explicitly.

  • @Primary on one bean makes it the default choice.
  • @Qualifier("smsNotifier") at the injection point names the bean wanted.
  • A parameter name that equals a bean name also works as a fallback.

Example: EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier both implement Notifier; mark Email as @Primary and ask for Sms by qualifier where needed.

No. Since Spring 4.3, a class with exactly one constructor gets it used for injection automatically, so @Autowired is optional there.

You still need it when a class has several constructors and you want to tell Spring which one to use, or on setter and field injection. Kotlin and Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor rely on this single-constructor rule to keep classes short.

@Service
class OrderService {
  OrderService(Notifier n) { ... }   // injected, no annotation
}

Ask for a collection of the interface type and Spring injects every matching bean.

OrderService(List<Notifier> all) { ... }
OrderService(Map<String, Notifier> byName) { ... }

With a List the beans come in order (use @Order to control it); with a Map the key is the bean name, e.g. emailNotifier. This is the usual way to build a strategy registry or a plugin chain without an if-else.

code.title: Singleton holding a prototype: stale vs provider

followUps:
A scoped proxy is a small stand-in object injected in place of a short-lived bean, which looks up the real instance each time you call it.

Example: a singleton service needs the request-scoped UserContext. At startup there is no request, so Spring injects a proxy (@Scope(value="request", proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS)). Each method call on the proxy finds the current request's real bean and forwards to it. The alternative is ObjectProvider<UserContext> and calling getObject() yourself.

Request scope is stored in a thread-local tied to the thread that received the HTTP request. A new thread has no such request, so the lookup fails with IllegalStateException: No thread-bound request found.

This hits @Async methods, executor tasks and parallel streams. The fix is to read the values you need on the request thread and pass them as plain arguments, or to copy the context explicitly with a task decorator. Never rely on the request bean inside the new thread.

The proxy is created in the last step of initialisation, inside postProcessAfterInitialization of a BeanPostProcessor, after your @PostConstruct has run.

The post-processor (Spring's auto-proxy creator) sees your finished bean, finds that it has @Transactional methods, and returns a proxy that wraps it instead. The container stores the proxy under the bean name, so other beans get the proxy. This is also why your own @PostConstruct code runs on the raw object, without a transaction.

Start it in a lifecycle callback after dependencies are set, and stop it in the destroy callback, so it follows the context's life.

  • Start in @PostConstruct or, better, in a SmartLifecycle.start() or an ApplicationReadyEvent listener, when the whole app is ready.
  • Stop in @PreDestroy or SmartLifecycle.stop(): interrupt the thread and join it with a timeout.

Prefer a managed ExecutorService or @Scheduled over raw threads; Spring then shuts them down for you.

Write a class annotated @AutoConfiguration with conditional beans, and list it in a file inside a library. Users then only add your dependency.

  1. Create module acme-spring-boot-autoconfigure with the config class, using @ConditionalOnMissingBean so users can override your beans.
  2. Bind settings with @ConfigurationProperties("acme").
  3. Add the class name to META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.
  4. Create the starter module acme-spring-boot-starter: an empty jar that depends on the autoconfigure module and the libraries needed.

Exclude it by class name, either in code or in a property.

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
// or application.yml:
// spring.autoconfigure.exclude: org.springframework...DataSourceAutoConfiguration

Use excludeName when the class is not on the compile classpath. Another way is to define your own bean of the same type, because most auto-configurations use @ConditionalOnMissingBean and back off. Check the result with --debug: it lists the exclusion under "Exclusions".

code.title: Proxy advice and the self-invocation gap

followUps:
JDK proxies work only for interfaces; CGLIB works by subclassing, so it can proxy a class without an interface.

JDKCGLIB
Needsan interfacenon-final class
Proxy isa sibling of the targeta subclass of the target
Can't advisemethods not on the interfacefinal and private methods

Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true), so injecting by the concrete class works.

Because the call goes this.method() inside the object, it never passes through the proxy, and the transaction logic lives only in the proxy.

In the program above, calling proxy.outer() prints BEGIN/COMMIT only once; the inner call runs without its own. Fixes: move the method to another bean and inject it, split the class, or inject self (rarely nice). AspectJ weaving also works because it changes the bytecode itself.

A filter is plain servlet code that runs before Spring MVC; an interceptor is Spring MVC code that runs after the handler is chosen. So an interceptor knows the controller method, a filter does not.

Use a filter for things that apply to every request, including static files and error pages (CORS, request id, compression, auth). Use an interceptor when you need the handler, for example to read a custom annotation on the method. Interceptors cannot wrap the servlet itself or change the request object the way a filter can.

Filters run first and 404, 405 and 415 come from the DispatcherServlet's lookup, not from your controller.

  • 404: no handler mapping matches the path (a missing static resource also counts).
  • 405: the path matches, but not for this HTTP method, e.g. a POST to a @GetMapping.
  • 415: the path and method match, but no converter can read the request's Content-Type (for example text/plain sent to a JSON endpoint).

A malformed JSON body is 400 and a failed @Valid is 400 as well.

Spring Security is itself a servlet filter, so it sits at the very start of the chain, before the DispatcherServlet.

Spring registers one DelegatingFilterProxy/FilterChainProxy, which holds a SecurityFilterChain of about a dozen internal filters (CSRF, authentication, authorization). This is why a request without a valid login is rejected with 401/403 before any controller or interceptor runs. Method-level rules such as @PreAuthorize are different: they are AOP advice on beans.

For one incoming request: filters, then the interceptor's preHandle, then the controller, with aspects around the beans it calls.

  1. Servlet filters (Security first, by their order).
  2. DispatcherServlet picks the handler.
  3. Interceptor preHandle.
  4. Controller method, then aspect advice on any service it calls.
  5. Interceptor postHandle, response written, afterCompletion.
  6. Filters unwind in reverse order.

Aspects fire at step 4, whenever a proxied method is actually called.

A projection is a query result that contains only some columns, returned as an interface or a record instead of the full entity.

interface UserView { String getName(); String getEmail(); }
List<UserView> findByActiveTrue();

Spring Data generates a SELECT name, email only, which is faster and lighter than loading all 30 columns and the lazy associations. Projections are also not managed, so no dirty checking applies. Class-based (DTO) projections work with constructors, and dynamic ones with a generic Class<T> parameter.

Because save() must decide between INSERT and UPDATE, and for an entity with an id that was set by hand it asks the database whether the row exists.

Spring Data calls isNew(): if the id is null (or the version attribute is null) it does persist; otherwise merge, and merge loads the row first (a SELECT). With ids you assign yourself, add a @Version field or implement Persistable to avoid the extra query. Generated ids do not have this cost.

code.title: Persistence context and dirty checking

followUps:
Flush sends the pending SQL to the database; commit then ends the transaction and makes those changes permanent for others.

After a flush the changes are still invisible to other transactions and can still be rolled back. Hibernate flushes automatically before a commit, and before a query that might touch changed tables (FlushMode.AUTO). Example: you change an email, run a JPQL query on users, Hibernate flushes the UPDATE first so the query sees it, but nothing is committed until the method ends.

Open-in-view keeps the EntityManager open until the response has been written, so lazy fields can load in the controller or while Jackson renders JSON.

It is controversial because the database connection is held for the whole request, including slow rendering, and lazy loading hidden in the view layer causes N+1 queries nobody sees in the service code. Spring Boot enables it by default and logs a warning. Most teams set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false and fetch what they need in the service, returning DTOs.

code.title: N+1 queries counted versus a batched fetch

followUps:
EAGER only moves the extra queries to a different place and often makes them worse, because it loads the association every time, even when you do not need it.

With findAll() on 100 authors, EAGER still runs one extra query per author, since a derived query is not a join. Now every other use of Author also pays for the books. Keep associations LAZY and fetch them for the specific use case with join fetch or @EntityGraph.

Count the SQL statements in a test and fail the build when the number goes above the expected one.

  • Enable Hibernate statistics (hibernate.generate_statistics=true) and read getPrepareStatementCount() before and after the call.
  • Or use a datasource proxy library with an assertion helper.
stats.clear();
service.listAuthorsWithBooks();
assertEquals(2, stats.getPrepareStatementCount());

Use realistic data (several parents), since one parent hides N+1.

The inner method marks the shared transaction as rollback-only. When the outer code catches the exception and carries on, the commit at the end fails with UnexpectedRollbackException.

With REQUIRED there is just one transaction. The inner proxy sees the exception and sets the flag; the outer cannot clear it. To keep the outer work, run the inner call in REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED (savepoint), or catch the exception inside a smaller transaction of its own.

Each request that uses REQUIRES_NEW holds two connections at once, so the pool needs more than the thread count, or the nesting must be removed.

The safe rule from the pool-exhaustion guidance: pool size at least threads * (max connections per request - 1) + 1. With 10 request threads and 2 connections each, 11 avoids the deadlock; 20 is fully safe. In the program above, a pool of 2 with 2 requests times out. Better still, move the audit write to an event after commit.

Run the code through a real Spring context and check whether a transaction is active, or whether the change is rolled back.

  • Call the bean from a test (without a test-level @Transactional, which would hide the problem) and assert that TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() is true inside, e.g. via a spy.
  • Throw an exception and check that the data was not saved.
  • Check that the bean is a proxy: AopUtils.isAopProxy(service).

Setting logging.level.org.springframework.transaction=TRACE shows the begin and commit lines.

readOnly=true tells Spring and the database that the method will not change data, which allows some savings, but it does not forbid writes by itself.

In Hibernate it sets the flush mode to MANUAL, so there is no dirty checking at the end and less memory is used. The JDBC driver or database may route the query to a read replica or optimise the connection. It is a hint, not security: a native UPDATE may still run on some databases. Use it on query-only service methods.

@Value injects one property into one field; @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole group of properties into a typed object, which is better for anything beyond a single setting.

@ConfigurationProperties("mail")
@Validated
record MailProps(@NotBlank String host, int port) {}

It supports relaxed names (MAIL_HOST equals mail.host), validation at startup, nesting, lists and IDE hints. With @Value a typo in the key is found only at runtime, and it does not bind objects.

Use a database that accepts two passwords at once during the change, then switch the app, then remove the old one.

  1. Create the new credential (a second user, or a dual-password feature).
  2. Put it in the secret store and roll out the app gradually (rolling restart), so old and new pods both work.
  3. When no pod uses the old password, revoke it.

Vault's dynamic database credentials do this automatically with short leases. The Hikari pool should be recreated on restart, so keep maxLifetime shorter than the credential lifetime.

code.title: Connection pool starved by nested transactions

followUps:
Virtual threads remove the shortage of request threads, but not the shortage of database connections. The pool still has a fixed size, so waiting moves from a platform thread to a parked virtual thread.

You can now accept 10,000 concurrent requests cheaply, and all of them queue for 20 connections. Without limits the queue and latency grow. Keep a bounded pool and connection timeout, add a semaphore or bulkhead around DB-heavy work, and avoid holding locks (synchronized pinning) while blocking.

Start from what the database can run in parallel, not from the number of app threads. A small pool is usually faster.

A useful starting formula: connections = (CPU cores * 2) + disk spindles, which gives about 10 to 20 for one database server. Then measure: with 100 requests per second and 20 ms of database time per request, you need about 100 * 0.02 = 2 connections busy on average. Add headroom, set a short connectionTimeout, and watch hikaricp.connections.pending. Total across all app instances must stay below the database limit.

Put validation at several levels, each checking what it knows: format at the edge, business rules in the service, invariants in the domain.

  • Controller: @Valid on the DTO for shape (required, length, format), answered with 400.
  • Service: rules that need data, such as "email not taken" or "enough stock".
  • Domain: invariants that must always hold, e.g. an Order constructor rejecting a negative total.

The database constraints (unique, not null) are the last safety net.

Write an integration test that calls the service through the Spring context and checks both the commit and the rollback paths, including the failure of a later step.

  1. Use @SpringBootTest with a real or Testcontainers database.
  2. Do not put @Transactional on the test itself, or the test wraps everything in one transaction.
  3. Call the use case, force a failure in the last step, and assert that the first step's rows are gone.
  4. Assert that the audit row from REQUIRES_NEW is still there.

Add an ArchUnit test for the dependency direction.
